catalog_quote: [p. 48] According to Munro and Lopez (1999), the last syllable of uninflected words is stressed in Quiaviní Zapotec. ... [p. 74] In Quiaviní Zapotec, neither prefixes nor suffixes are ever stressed. ... In order to show that Quiaviní Zapotec prominence pays attention to morphological domains, examples with the diminutive suffix and clitics demonstrate that stress is not simply word-final; in these examples, stress is still located on the root syllable ... (36) / [ba̰t]-eʔ / → [ ba̰.teʔ] 'little skunk' ... [p. 75] All in all, the data above illustrate that affixes have no effect on stress location. Compounds illustrate the final root (morphological) prominence. When two roots are attached to form a compound, prominence is located on the second root. ... [p. 78] Quiaviní Zapotec shows culminativity in that there is only one prominent syllable per word, and demarcativity in that the (final) root syllable is always prominent. ... [p. 85] (67) ALIGN (Hd(Ft), R, Root, R) (ALIGN-R) 'For every stressed syllable (= head of a foot) there must be some root such that the right edge of that syllable matches the right edge of the root' ... [p. 101] In disyllabic and longer words, Quiaviní Zapotec displays a trochaic metrical pattern at the moraic and syllabic level. Further, in accordance with Munro and Lopez (1999), stress is demarcative, with the root-final syllable consistently carrying prominence.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: sanj1284 is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title turned up two Glottolog title-hits that are one and the same work: Chávez Peón's 2010 UBC dissertation on Quiaviní Zapotec prosody (Glottolog 575961 and duplicate 605100). It was already held by the project from our earlier reading at (PDF with text layer; no scanned needed) and I read chapter 3 in full. It is a first-hand, fieldwork-based statement: stress is culminative and demarcative, falling on the root-final syllable (affixes and clitics never stressed; second root in compounds; last syllable of polysyllabic loan roots, with <10 loanword exceptions), analysed as quantity-sensitive moraic trochees with ALIGN-R to the root; duration is the main acoustic cue. It cites Munro & Lopez (1999) for the earlier generalisation 'the last syllable of uninflected words is stressed'. The same author's CLA 2008 proceedings paper (also held by the project, p.2 and p.13) repeats the last-syllable-of-uninflected-words statement and supplies the acoustic evidence. Nothing new was downloaded; no items remain unread, so no acquisition priorities. Appended a dated search note with verified page locators to in that directory. If the language is added to the catalog, Chávez Peón 2010 p.78/p.101 is the deciding source: fixed root-final (surface: final) stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: One stress per (content) word, on the final syllable of the root: native roots are mostly monosyllabic, so stress is word-final in prefix+root words and in etymologically opaque or borrowed polysyllables (last syllable of uninflected words = Munro & Lopez's 'key syllable'), but the diminutive suffix and enclitics are unstressed, so stress is root-final rather than word-final; in compounds the last root is stressed. Formalised as ALIGN(Hd(Ft), R, Root, R) with quantity-sensitive moraic trochees; the stressed syllable must be bimoraic (vowel lengthening before lenis coda/open syllable, fortis codas moraic). Main acoustic correlate is duration (Chávez-Peón 2008).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; culminative single prominence per word. Function words (articles, clitics, some adverbs) 'do not need to be stressed' and are prosodically dependent on content words (p. 49).
new_statements.exceptions: Diminutive suffix -eʔ and clitics never stressed (stress stays on root: [ˈla.teʔ] 'little can', p. 74/84); loanwords keep the Spanish stressed syllable as the prominent syllable and delete post-tonic final open-syllable vowels so that the head is root-final (p. 94-95); tone contours, diphthongs and non-modal phonation restricted to stressed (root) syllables. Note the Teotitlán del Valle variety (Uchihara & Gutiérrez 2020: 15) instead places accent on the last syllable of the phonological word including the diminutive suffix.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word = content word (root plus affixes/clitics); examples are citation forms of nouns, verbs, adjectives; the 2008 CLA study measured target words in carrier sentences. Language is tonal (4 tones) with contrastive phonation; stress is independent of tone (tone language with a stress statement would also apply, but the location rule is root-final).
new_statements.identity_note: The primary statement (Chávez Peón 2010, 2008; Uchihara & Pérez Báez 2016) describes San Lucas Quiaviní Zapotec, a Tlacolula Valley variety that Glottolog files under sanj1284 (no separate dialect code in Glottolog 5.1's dialect list held by the project). Uchihara & Gutiérrez 2020 describes Teotitlán del Valle Zapotec (Glottolog dialect teot1238 under sanj1284) and differs in one detail: there the accent falls on the last syllable of the phonological word including the diminutive suffix (bεˈl:εˀn 'little fish'), whereas in Quiaviní the diminutive suffix and clitics are unstressed and stress stays on the root-final syllable ([ˈla.teʔ] 'little can'). Knudson & Jones 1977 (not reachable) describes San Juan Guelavía (sanj1289).

new_statements.reading: Word stress in (San Lucas Quiaviní) Western Tlacolula Valley Zapotec is morphologically fixed on the final syllable of the root: one stress per word; prefixes, suffixes and enclitics never carry it; in compounds it falls on the second (final) root; polysyllabic loan roots are stressed on their last syllable because Spanish post-tonic final vowels are deleted, with fewer than ten lexical exceptions where the Spanish stressed syllable stays non-final. Since native roots are almost all monosyllabic, the surface pattern is 'stress on the root (= last syllable of uninflected words, Munro & Lopez 1999)'. Foot structure is analysed as quantity-sensitive moraic trochees aligned to the right edge of the root (ALIGN-R); duration is the main acoustic correlate. Classification-wise: fixed stress on the root-final syllable (morphologically conditioned, not phonologically word-final).

new_statements.relation_note: Same ISO language (zab) but a different town variety (Teotitlán del Valle, TdVZ), not San Lucas Quiaviní. Agrees with the catalog that prefixes and clitics are never stressed and that the last root of a compound carries stress; DIFFERS in that a suffix forming its own syllable takes the prominence (comitative -nǣ, affective =æ’ny: ri.git.ˈnǣ, gú.ˈnæ’n), whereas Chávez Peón 2010 says SLQZ suffixes (incl. the diminutive) are never stressed and stress stays on the root. Surface generalization for TdVZ is 'last syllable of the p-word' rather than 'root'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Teotitlán del Valle Zapotec: exactly one prominent ('stressed', marked ˈ) syllable per phonological word; it is the last syllable of the p-word = root + affixes, clitics excluded: root in prefix+root words (ri.ˈzu, gu.ˈza, ba.ˈlǎw), the suffix in root+suffix words (ri.git.ˈnǣ, gú.ˈnæ’n), the last root in compounds (bed(y).ˈgǐdy, ru.kwa.ˈdyag). The prominent syllable must be bimoraic (long vowel or short vowel + fortis coda); prominence licenses contour tones, laryngealized/glottalized vowels and vowel length; non-prominent syllables neutralize these.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: one and only one prominent syllable per p-word. Free function words and discourse interrogatives carry their own accent (p. 36, p. 108); in noun+adjective and verb+noun sequences each member keeps its prominence and forms its own p-word (p. 49).
new_statements.exceptions: Table 2.8 features are 'for the prototypical cases, and exceptions do exist' (p. 31); proclitics, especially negators, acquire prominence when they host a second-position clitic (p. 49); the affective/diminutive suffix takes prominence even though it is clitic-like in distribution (p. 36).
new_statements.identity_note: The catalog record and existing statements are San Lucas Quiaviní Zapotec (Chávez Peón 2010). Work 0 describes Teotitlán del Valle Zapotec (ISO zab, self-identified in the abstract), works 1/4 San Juan Guelavía Zapotec (the type variety of sanj1284), work 3 Santa Ana del Valle Zapotec; all are town varieties of the one ISO language zab / Glottolog sanj1284, and the stress formulations differ by variety and by analysis.

new_statements.quote: A word consists of one or more syllables, only one of which is stressed. Stress affects a syllable in a variety of ways, tending to raise the pitch of the syllable, to lengthen fortis consonants, and to lengthen or cause rearticulation of vowels. In the majority of words, stress tends to be in the penultimate syllable and is left unmarked in illustrations when so occurring. [p. 163] … When a high front vocoid occurs as a final member of a syllable onset, however, the only criterion available is stress placement. In words such as /štyu/ [štyú:] shame, for example, where stress is on the /u/ (causing it to be phonetically long), we consider the high front vocoid to be a semivowel, part of the margin. [p. 178]

new_statements.relation_note: San Juan Guelavía is the type variety of sanj1284/zab. The chapter states penultimate stress for most words, against the catalog's root-final (= last syllable of uninflected words) placement from Chávez Peón 2010 for SLQZ. Part of the gap is analytic rather than empirical: Jones & Knudson syllabify rearticulated and clustered vowels as two syllables ([byo?on] 'we went', /štieš/ 'garlic'), which the SLQZ analyses treat as one syllable with a complex vowel nucleus, so 'penultimate' there often corresponds to the SLQZ 'final/root' syllable; the note on stressed vowels being lengthened/rearticulated also matches Chávez Peón's duration cue. This is my interpretation, not a claim in the source.
new_statements.rule_in_words: San Juan Guelavía Zapotec (1977 analysis): one stressed syllable per word; in the majority of words it is the penultimate syllable (left unmarked), other placements being marked with an accent in the examples (e.g. /štyu/ [štyú:] 'shame', final). Correlates: higher pitch, lengthening of fortis consonants, lengthening or rearticulation of the vowel; stressed oral vowels are long before lenis consonants or pause; laryngeal vowels are rearticulated when stressed. Tone is a separate three-level register system, with a raised allotone under stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned ('only one of which is stressed').
new_statements.exceptions: Stress only 'tends to be' penultimate 'in the majority of words'; non-penultimate stress occurs and is marked (e.g. /štyu/ [štyú:] 'shame' with final stress; /štieš/ [šti:ɛš:] 'garlic' with stress on the first vowel of a cluster).

readall_conflicts: Three town varieties of zab get three formulations. Chávez Peón 2010 (catalog, San Lucas Quiaviní): stress on the root-final syllable, affixes and clitics never stressed, hence last syllable of uninflected words. Gutiérrez Lorenzo 2021 (Teotitlán del Valle): one prominent syllable per phonological word, the LAST syllable of root+affixes: root after prefixes, but the SUFFIX when root and suffix are separate syllables (ri.git.ˈnǣ, gú.ˈnæ’n), last root in compounds; this contradicts the SLQZ claim that suffixes (incl. the diminutive) are never stressed, so either the dialects differ or the SLQZ generalization is too strong. Jones & Knudson 1977 (San Juan Guelavía): stress 'tends to be in the penultimate syllable' in the majority of words, one stress per word, exceptions marked; this contradicts both, but their syllabification treats rearticulated/clustered vowels as two syllables ([byo?on] 'we went', /štieš/ 'garlic'), so many of their 'penultimate' cases are the single final/root syllable of the later analyses (my interpretation, flagged as such). All sources agree on culminativity (one stress per word), on prefixes never being stressed, and on duration/rearticulation as a main correlate. Esposito 2003 (Santa Ana del Valle) is silent; Lillehaugen 2006 could not be opened.

sources.note: §5 p.15 (Teotitlán del Valle variety): 'accent is culminative and obligatory; there is only one accent per phonological word.. The accent falls on the last syllable of the phonological word, which consists of a root plus an optional prefix or suffix, or of a compounded root'; diminutive suffix shifts accent (bεˈl:εˀn); enclitics lack accent; pitch not a reliable correlate, duration is.
